scenes.visual: Title card 'One Door for Two Cycles' over a close-up of one oak leaf with a single tiny opening. COLOUR MAP (both films): the air is a clear glass TUB labelled 'air' with a TEAL level marker and a ppm readout; GREEN arrows = photosynthesis (carbon out of the air); ORANGE arrows = respiration (in); BROWN arrows = decomposition (in); RED arrow = burning fossil fuels (in); DARK BLUE two-way arrow = ocean; LIGHT BLUE arrows and drops = water. Anchor organism: one big cartoon oak in a Virginia yard, with a deer and a rotting log. All drawings are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; any curve drawn from the 2025 Mauna Loa monthly values is labelled 'data: NOAA and Scripps, Mauna Loa'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Same oak, yard, tub and colours as the first film.

scenes.tts: Can a dry summer change the carbon dioxide in the air? To answer that, we have to follow water, not carbon.
scenes.visual: The oak in a parched yard under a hot sun; cracked soil. The air TUB from the first film floats above with its TEAL marker. Question card: 'Can a dry summer change the air's carbon dioxide?'
scenes.narration: Can a dry summer change the carbon dioxide in the air? To answer that, we have to follow water, not carbon.

scenes.tts: The first film showed the air as a tub of carbon. The oak's green arrow drained it every summer. Now follow the oak's water instead.
scenes.visual: Quick replay: the GREEN 'photosynthesis' arrow runs from the tub into the oak and the marker drops. Then the tub slides to the top corner and stays there, small, for the rest of the film. LIGHT BLUE drops appear in the soil.
scenes.narration: The first film showed the air as a tub of carbon. The oak's green arrow drained it every summer. Now follow the oak's water instead.

scenes.tts: Rain falls on the yard. That is precipitation. Some of it soaks into the ground, which is infiltration. Some flows downhill to a stream. That is runoff.
scenes.visual: A rain cloud over the yard; LIGHT BLUE drops fall, word 'precipitation' appears. Drops sink into the soil, word 'infiltration'. A sheet of water runs down a slope into a stream, word 'runoff'.
scenes.narration: Rain falls on the yard. That is precipitation. Some of it soaks into the ground, which is infiltration. Some flows downhill to a stream. That is runoff.

scenes.tts: The oak's roots take water from the soil. It moves up the stem to the leaves. Then it leaves through tiny openings in the leaves, as water vapor. That is transpiration.
scenes.visual: Cutaway oak: LIGHT BLUE dots enter the roots, travel up the trunk and out along branches to the leaves, then puff out of the leaves as faint vapour wisps. Word 'transpiration' appears with an arrow to the wisps.
scenes.narration: The oak's roots take water from the soil. It moves up the stem to the leaves. Then it leaves through tiny openings in the leaves, as water vapor. That is transpiration.

scenes.tts: Water also evaporates from the pond, and most of all from the ocean. High up, the vapor cools into tiny droplets that form clouds. That is condensation. Then rain falls again.
scenes.visual: Vapour wisps rise from a pond, and thicker wisps from a strip of ocean at the screen edge, word 'evaporation' (ocean wisps drawn biggest). Wisps meet high up and bead into a cloud, word 'condensation'. Rain begins again, closing the loop; the six words now sit around a circle.
scenes.narration: Water also evaporates from the pond, and most of all from the ocean. High up, the vapor cools into tiny droplets that form clouds. That is condensation. Then rain falls again.

scenes.tts: Plants move a lot of this water. One study estimated that nearly two thirds of the water moving from land into the air goes through plants. The estimate has a wide range.
scenes.visual: A bar labelled 'water moving from land into the air', about two-thirds shaded GREEN-leaf pattern labelled 'through plants (one study's estimate)', with a wide error bracket labelled 'wide range'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Plants move a lot of this water. One study estimated that nearly two thirds of the water moving from land into the air goes through plants. The estimate has a wide range.

scenes.tts: Now zoom into one leaf. Carbon dioxide comes in through the same tiny openings that water vapor goes out of. One door serves both cycles.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one leaf surface, then onto one tiny opening drawn as two curved lips (cartoon, labelled 'tiny opening, schematic'). LIGHT BLUE vapour arrows stream out; GREEN-outlined arrows labelled 'carbon dioxide' stream in through the same gap. Label above the gap: 'one door'.
scenes.narration: Now zoom into one leaf. Carbon dioxide comes in through the same tiny openings that water vapor goes out of. One door serves both cycles.

scenes.tts: Inside the leaf, photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together to make sugar. The water came up from the roots. The carbon dioxide came in through the door.
scenes.visual: Inside the leaf, a LIGHT BLUE stream from below and a GREEN carbon dioxide stream from the opening meet at a box labelled 'photosynthesis'; sugar cubes come out. Path labels: 'from the roots' and 'through the door'.
scenes.narration: Inside the leaf, photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together to make sugar. The water came up from the roots. The carbon dioxide came in through the door.

scenes.tts: Now a hot, dry summer. The soil dries out, and the oak closes its tiny openings to save water. What happens to the green arrow on the air tub? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: Sun intensifies; soil cracks; root dots thin out. The tiny opening's lips squeeze nearly shut. The small air tub in the corner pulses, its GREEN arrow outlined with a question mark. Question card: 'Green arrow: thicker, thinner or the same?'
scenes.narration: Now a hot, dry summer. The soil dries out, and the oak closes its tiny openings to save water. What happens to the green arrow on the air tub? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: It gets thinner. With the openings nearly closed, less carbon dioxide gets in. So the oak takes less carbon out of the air.
scenes.visual: Through the nearly closed opening, only one thin vapour arrow goes out and one thin carbon dioxide arrow comes in. In the corner tub, the GREEN arrow shrinks to a thread.
scenes.narration: It gets thinner. With the openings nearly closed, less carbon dioxide gets in. So the oak takes less carbon out of the air.

scenes.tts: This happens in real forests. In two thousand three, Europe had a very hot, dry summer. One study estimated that plants there took in about thirty percent less carbon than usual.
scenes.caption: This happens in real forests. In 2003, Europe had a very hot, dry summer. One study estimated that plants there took in about 30 percent less carbon than usual.
scenes.visual: Cartoon map outline of Europe in summer orange, label '2003: very hot, dry summer'. Two bars: 'usual carbon taken in' and a shorter bar 'about 30% less (one study's estimate)'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: This happens in real forests. In 2003, Europe had a very hot, dry summer. One study estimated that plants there took in about 30 percent less carbon than usual.

scenes.tts: One thing in this picture does not cycle. Carbon and water go around and around, used again and again. Energy does not. It comes in as sunlight and leaves as heat, so plants need new sunlight every day.
scenes.visual: Carbon and water loops spin as two circles (GREEN/ORANGE and LIGHT BLUE). A straight yellow arrow 'sunlight' enters the oak from one side and a wavy red-orange arrow 'heat' leaves the other side, never curving back. Label: 'matter cycles; energy flows through'.
scenes.narration: One thing in this picture does not cycle. Carbon and water go around and around, used again and again. Energy does not. It comes in as sunlight and leaves as heat, so plants need new sunlight every day.

scenes.tts: The two cycles are linked at the leaf. Water going out and carbon dioxide coming in pass through the same tiny openings. So a change in one cycle can change the other.
scenes.visual: Back to the single tiny opening, now wide again after rain: LIGHT BLUE out, carbon dioxide in. The water circle and the carbon circle overlap at the opening, the overlap glowing.
scenes.narration: The two cycles are linked at the leaf. Water going out and carbon dioxide coming in pass through the same tiny openings. So a change in one cycle can change the other.

scenes.visual: End card, one line only: 'Water out and carbon in use the same door.'
